title: Engineering Graphics/CAD
description: Builds fluency in engineering drawing standards, orthographic and pictorial projection, section and auxiliary views, dimensioning and GD&T, fits and finishes, 2D drafting, 3D solid modeling, assemblies and BOMs, and professional CAD review workflows.

topics.title: Engineering Drawing Standards (ANSI/ISO)
topics.description: Engineering graphics begins with shared drawing conventions. Standards let designers, manufacturers, reviewers, and field teams interpret drawings consistently.

children.title: Purpose of standards
children.description: Students learn why engineering drawings are governed by conventions rather than personal preference.

children.title: Sheet organization
children.description: A drawing sheet organizes information so a reader can quickly understand the part, assembly, scale, and revision state.

children.title: Line types and lettering
children.description: Line types and lettering make geometry, hidden features, centers, and annotations readable.

children.title: Object, hidden, center, and construction lines
ANSI/ISO comparison
children.description: Students learn that drawing standards vary by region and organization, so standards must be identified explicitly.

topics.title: Orthographic Projection
topics.description: Orthographic projection is the core skill for representing 3D objects with precise 2D views that can be manufactured, inspected, or modeled.

children.title: Principal views
children.description: Students learn how front, top, and side views describe object shape without perspective distortion.

children.title: Projection theory
children.description: Projection theory explains how points, edges, and surfaces map from 3D space to drawing planes.

children.title: View selection
children.description: Good drawings use enough views to define the part without cluttering the sheet.

children.title: Reading orthographic drawings
children.description: Students practice mentally reconstructing 3D form from 2D views.

topics.title: Isometric and Pictorial Drawings
topics.description: Pictorial drawings help communicate form quickly. They are less precise than orthographic drawings, but excellent for visualization and design communication.

children.title: Isometric projection
children.description: Isometric views show three dimensions at once while preserving a consistent axis system.

children.title: Oblique and perspective views
children.description: Other pictorial methods help students understand when technical communication should prioritize clarity over measurement.

children.title: Freehand technical sketching
children.description: Sketching develops spatial reasoning before software becomes the main tool.

children.title: Design communication uses
children.description: Students learn when pictorial drawings support concept explanation, assembly understanding, or presentation.

topics.title: Sectioning and Auxiliary Views
topics.description: Section and auxiliary views reveal geometry that ordinary views cannot show clearly, especially internal features and inclined surfaces.

children.title: Full, half, and offset sections
children.description: Section views cut through an object to show internal structure without excessive hidden lines.

children.title: Broken-out and revolved sections
children.description: Partial section methods reveal local details while preserving the rest of the view.

children.title: Auxiliary views
children.description: Auxiliary views show inclined surfaces in true size and shape.

children.title: Choosing advanced views
children.description: Students learn to choose view types based on what the reader needs to understand.

topics.title: Dimensioning and Tolerancing (GD&T)
topics.description: Dimensions and tolerances convert geometry into manufacturing and inspection requirements. This topic turns drawings from pictures into controlled engineering documents.

children.title: Dimensioning principles
children.description: Good dimensions define size and location clearly without duplication or contradictions.

children.title: Tolerance types
children.description: Tolerances communicate allowable variation, which is essential because no part is manufactured perfectly.

children.title: GD&T foundations
children.description: GD&T controls form, orientation, location, and runout using symbolic language.

children.title: Inspection thinking
children.description: Students learn that tolerances must be measurable, not merely written on a drawing.

topics.title: Fits and Surface Finishes
topics.description: Fits and finishes connect drawings to how parts assemble, move, seal, wear, and perform after manufacturing.

children.title: Clearance, transition, and interference fits
children.description: Fit selection determines whether parts slide, locate, or press together.

children.title: Surface texture
children.description: Surface finish affects friction, sealing, fatigue, coating, and appearance.

children.title: Manufacturing process implications
children.description: Finish and fit requirements should match realistic manufacturing methods.

children.title: Cost and performance tradeoffs
children.description: Tighter tolerances and smoother finishes cost more, so students learn to specify only what function requires.

topics.title: CAD Software Interface (SolidWorks/AutoCAD)
topics.description: CAD fluency begins with understanding the software workspace, command structure, file types, and modeling/drafting workflow.

children.title: CAD workspace orientation
children.description: Students learn how to move confidently through menus, toolbars, view controls, and feature/history panels.

children.title: Sketch and drawing setup
children.description: Setup choices determine units, scale, constraints, and drawing readability.

children.title: Constraints and relations
children.description: Constraints make geometry intentional rather than accidental.

children.title: Horizontal, vertical, parallel, and perpendicular constraints
File types and interoperability
children.description: Engineering teams exchange models and drawings across software, so students need basic file literacy.

topics.title: 2D Drafting
topics.description: 2D drafting remains essential for layouts, manufacturing drawings, construction drawings, and quick technical communication.

children.title: Basic drawing commands
children.description: Students learn to create accurate geometry through commands rather than approximate visual placement.

children.title: Layers and annotation
children.description: Layers and annotation keep drawings readable and controllable.

children.title: Dimensioning in CAD
children.description: Digital dimensioning connects drawing geometry to standards and sheet readability.

children.title: Layouts and plotting
children.description: Students learn how drawings move from model space to a printable, reviewable sheet.

topics.title: 3D Solid Modeling
topics.description: Solid modeling lets students create parametric 3D parts that can generate drawings, assemblies, simulations, and manufacturing outputs.

children.title: Sketch-based features
children.description: Most solid models begin with constrained sketches that become 3D features.

children.title: Feature editing and design intent
children.description: A good model can change predictably because its features are organized around design intent.

children.title: Reference geometry
children.description: Reference geometry supports complex features and controlled part construction.

children.title: Model quality
children.description: Students learn habits that keep models stable, readable, and reusable.

topics.title: Assembly Drawings and Bill of Materials
topics.description: Assemblies show how parts fit and function together. BOMs connect models and drawings to purchasing, manufacturing, and documentation.

children.title: Assembly constraints and mates
children.description: Constraints define how components relate, move, or lock together.

children.title: Exploded views
children.description: Exploded views communicate assembly sequence and part relationships.

children.title: Assembly drawings
children.description: Assembly drawings present component relationships, fasteners, references, and critical dimensions.

children.title: Bill of materials
children.description: A BOM translates the assembly into a structured list of parts and quantities.

topics.title: Parametric, BIM, and Digital Workflow Basics
topics.description: Modern CAD work increasingly includes parametric constraints, cloud collaboration, and BIM-style model information. This extension keeps the course current without replacing engineering graphics fundamentals.

children.title: Parametric modeling concepts
children.description: Students learn how dimensions, constraints, and variables can drive design changes.

children.title: BIM concepts
children.description: BIM introduces object-based modeling where geometry carries metadata and documentation relationships.

children.title: Digital workflow
children.description: Students learn how models, drawings, exports, and reviews connect in a real project workflow.

children.title: PDF, STEP, and drawing package delivery
Intro to digital fabrication
children.description: Fabrication awareness helps students model geometry that can actually be cut, printed, machined, or assembled.

topics.title: Design Review, File Management, and Fabrication Readiness
topics.description: The final topic focuses on professional habits: checking drawings, organizing files, preparing deliverables, and communicating design decisions clearly.

children.title: Drawing review workflow
children.description: Review skills help students catch missing views, ambiguous dimensions, and inconsistent standards before release.

children.title: File organization
children.description: Clean file structures prevent lost work and broken references in CAD projects.

children.title: Fabrication readiness
children.description: Students learn to ask whether a model and drawing package are ready for manufacturing, prototyping, or construction.

children.title: Technical communication package
children.description: A complete package combines drawings, models, BOMs, notes, and review history into a coherent deliverable.
